chief_complaint: new headache, jaw pain when chewing, and high ESR
hpi_details: A 57-year-old male presents to the clinic with new headache, jaw pain when chewing, and high ESR. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
ideas: He thinks his jaw stiffness and temple pain might be coming from clenching his jaw and grinding his teeth at night due to work stress.
concerns: He is worried that this throbbing one-sided headache could be a warning sign of a stroke like his older brother had.
expectations: He hopes to get a referral for a head CT scan or a prescription for strong painkillers so he can get through his workday.

clinical_knowledge.topic: Giant Cell Arteritis evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Giant Cell Arteritis is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Suspected giant cell arteritis is a vision-threatening emergency: arrange same-day emergency specialist assessment and clinician-directed glucocorticoids without delaying treatment for confirmatory testing.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: new headache, jaw pain when chewing, and high ESR

Key HPI features: A 57-year-old male presents to the clinic with new headache, jaw pain when chewing, and high ESR. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
Objective/Exam findings: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Giant Cell Arteritis.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Giant Cell Arteritis.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Tension headache without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Missing visual or neurologic symptoms that require immediate emergency assessment to prevent irreversible vision loss or stroke.
management_principles: Arrange same-day emergency ophthalmology/rheumatology or emergency-department assessment; clinician-directed glucocorticoids should not be delayed for temporal-artery imaging or biopsy
Confirm with temporal-artery ultrasound and/or biopsy according to local pathway, while monitoring glucocorticoid toxicity and preventive care
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

teaching.one_liner: A large-vessel vasculitis in adults over 50 causing new headache, jaw claudication, and elevated inflammatory markers; it can rapidly threaten vision.
red_flags: Any new visual change, double vision, or transient vision loss: seek emergency care immediately
New focal neurologic deficit, severe sudden headache, or stroke-like symptoms

must_ask.say: Is this a new type of headache for you?
Does your jaw hurt when chewing?
Any vision changes or episodes of dark vision?

history.answer: I have had a worsening headache around my temples and pain in my jaw whenever I chew food.
The headache and jaw pain started about two weeks ago and have been gradually getting worse.
It has been constantly present for the past two weeks, and I have never had a headache like this before.
The pain is mainly located over my temples on both sides, but it feels more severe on the right side.
It is a continuous, throbbing, deep ache that I would rate as a seven out of ten.
It hurts all day long, but the throbbing is noticeably worse when I first wake up in the morning.
Brushing my hair or touching my temples makes it worse; lying down quietly helps a little, but nothing relieves it completely.
No, I have not seen any flashing lights, zigzag lines, or experienced numbness before the pain started.
I felt mildly nauseous once or twice, but I have not vomited and I do not have extreme sensitivity to light or noise.
No, I haven't had any eye tearing, redness, runny nose, or drooping of my eyelids.
I haven't had a high fever or a stiff neck, just a low warm feeling and general fatigue.
No, I haven't experienced any arm or leg weakness, numbness, difficulty speaking, confusion, or seizures.
My vision seems normal right now with no double vision or blackouts, but I am very scared about losing my eyesight.
Yes, after chewing food for a minute or two, my jaw muscles ache and cramp so badly that I have to stop chewing.
Yes, my scalp feels very tender, especially when I comb my hair or rest my head on a pillow.
I have noticed stiffness and aching across my shoulders and neck in the mornings, along with feeling very worn out.
No, I have not had any head trauma, falls, or recent blows to the head.
I took some over-the-counter acetaminophen a few times, but it did not provide any real relief.
I have not noticed any triggers like lack of sleep, stress, specific foods, or alcohol.
I have never been diagnosed with high blood pressure, and I do not take blood pressure pills or blood thinners.
No one else in my household has headaches, and we do not use any indoor gas or unvented space heaters.
No, I do not have any history of cancer, HIV infection, or immunosuppressive treatments.
My primary care doctor ran some routine blood work yesterday and told me that my inflammation marker, the ESR, was extremely high.

I thought I might just be clenching my jaw and grinding my teeth in my sleep because work has been so stressful lately. I'm really worried this pounding headache on the side of my head means I might be having a stroke like my older brother did.
I have always been healthy and have no history of chronic medical conditions.
I have never had any surgeries and have never been admitted to a hospital.
I do not take any prescription medications, regular over-the-counter drugs, or herbal supplements.
I do not have any known allergies to medications, foods, or environmental substances.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used any tobacco products.
I only have one or two glasses of beer socially on the weekend, if at all.
I work as an office administrator and live in an apartment with my wife.
There is no family history of aneurysms, early strokes, headaches, or autoimmune disorders.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 128/82 mmHg, heart rate 74/min, respiratory rate 16/min, temperature 37.1 C, oxygen saturation 98% on room air.
Prominent, thickened, and exquisitely tender right superficial temporal artery with reduced pulsation; left temporal and distal radial pulses are intact.
Pupils equal, round, and reactive to light; visual acuity intact; extraocular movements full without diplopia; fundoscopic examination shows sharp optic disc margins without pallor or papilledema.
Cranial nerves II through XII intact with symmetric facial movements and normal sensation.
Supple neck without nuchal rigidity; negative Kernig and Brudzinski signs.
No tenderness on palpation over bilateral maxillary and frontal sinuses.
Normal bulk and 5/5 muscle strength throughout bilateral upper and lower extremities.
Intact light touch and pinprick sensation bilaterally across all dermatomes.
Finger-to-nose and rapid alternating movements intact; steady, normal gait without ataxia.
Bilateral shoulder and hip joints demonstrate full passive and active range of motion without synovitis, swelling, or localized joint tenderness.
